fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it was a few things coming together. I'd spent a lot of my academic career at Princeton working on language agents, things like WebShop, ReAct, SWE-bench, where we were trying to get models to actually take actions in an environment rather than just produce text. And what became increasingly clear to me was that the hard problems weren't going to get solved in a lab setting. You can build a nice benchmark, you can show a model does well on it, but the gap between that and something that works reliably for a real person with a real problem is enormous. And you only discover what that gap looks like when you have real users, real data, real failure modes coming at you every day.

So that was one piece. I wanted to be somewhere agents were actually being deployed, where the research questions are grounded in what's breaking in production.

The second piece was the domain. Customer-facing agents are conversational, they have clear outcomes, there's real accountability. If the agent gets it wrong, somebody's flight doesn't get rebooked. That's a very honest environment for research. It forces you to care about reliability and not just capability.

And then honestly, the people. When I talked to Bret and Clay, I came away feeling like they understood that this is a research problem and not just a product problem. They weren't asking me to come wrap an API. They wanted to build the science of how you make these systems trustworthy. That combination, the right problem, real-world grounding, and a team that takes the research seriously, that was enough conviction for me.

opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of it came down to timing and to the people.

On timing: I'd spent years in academia working on language agents, models that don't just generate text but take actions, use tools, and reason over multiple steps. A lot of that was in fairly controlled settings: text games, web environments, benchmarks we built ourselves. By around 2023 it was clear the models had gotten good enough that this wasn't a toy problem anymore. Agents were going to show up in the real world, and the hard questions were shifting. It was no longer "can a model do this at all?" It was "can it do this reliably, thousands of times a day, with real customers, under real business rules?" That's a very different research problem, and it's hard to study from a university lab without real deployments.

So when I talked with Bret and Clay, what struck me was that they weren't treating this as a wrapper on top of a model. They saw that putting an agent in front of a company's customers is a hard technical problem. You need the agent to follow policies, take consequential actions, handle messy human conversations, and you need to be able to measure whether it's actually doing the right thing. That last part really pulled me in. Evaluation and reliability were things I cared about deeply, and here was a place where they weren't academic. Every mistake has a real cost.

The other piece was conviction about the domain. Customer experience sounds unglamorous at first, but it's one of the clearest places where agents can create value right now. Every company has it, the interactions are high volume, there's a clear notion of success, and there's a huge gap between how good it is today and how good it could be. It's a great proving ground for the broader idea of agents doing real work.

And then the team itself. Bret and Clay have built and scaled products many times, and they had a real respect for research. They didn't just want to ship features, they wanted to understand the problems deeply. That combination of research ambition and real-world grounding is rare, and it felt like the right place to take ideas I'd been working on for years and see them actually matter to people.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, it came down to a feeling that the problems I cared about had moved.

My whole research career has been about agents — before language models were any good, I was building systems that played text games, that read a manual and then acted in an environment. The reason I cared about that was never the games. It was this belief that language is the right interface for getting a machine to do something useful in the world. And for a long time that was a pretty lonely bet, because the models just weren't capable enough for anyone to take it seriously as a product.

Then suddenly they were. And what I noticed was that the hardest, most interesting questions had quietly relocated. Not "can the model reason," but "can you get a system to behave correctly, the ten-thousandth time, for a customer who's angry and phrasing things in a way no one anticipated, where a wrong answer costs the company real money." That's a reliability problem, an evaluation problem, a specification problem. And you genuinely cannot study it from the outside. I can write a benchmark in my lab and I will be wrong about what matters, because I'm inventing the distribution instead of observing it.

So part of the conviction was just wanting access to reality — real traffic, real failures, real consequences.

The other part was the people. When I talked to Bret and Clay, what struck me was that they weren't trying to build a demo that trends for a week. They were asking what it takes for a company to actually hand over something they care about to an agent. That's a much less glamorous question, and a much better one. I wanted to work on the less glamorous one.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me it came down to a few things.

I've spent a lot of my career on language models and agents, first at OpenAI on the early GPT work, and then at Princeton on how to get these models to take actions and not just generate text. By the time I was thinking about Sierra, it was clear the models were getting good enough that the real bottleneck wasn't "can the model say something fluent?" It was "can you trust it to do a job reliably, in a messy real-world setting, with real customers and real consequences?" That's a hard research problem, and it's hard to make progress on it from inside a lab, because the real failure modes only show up when you deploy.

Customer service turns out to be a great setting for that. It's open-ended language, but it's also full of policies, tools, and APIs, and you can tell right away whether the agent did the right thing. Did it follow the rules? Did it resolve the issue? Did it make something up? That tight feedback loop is rare, and I wanted to be somewhere that both cared about the research and was shipping to real businesses.

The other piece was the people. Bret and Clay had a very clear view of where this was going, and they were focused on building something that actually works for companies, not just a demo. When you're deciding whether to leave academia, even partially, you want to be around people who are both ambitious and grounded. I felt that here.

So the conviction was that agents are going to be a huge part of how people interact with companies, that the hard problems are about reliability and grounding, and that Sierra was the place where I could work on those problems with real data and real stakes.

haiku-5.5.text:
Honestly, it came down to a gap I kept seeing. Models can look impressive in a demo or on a benchmark, but customers don't care about benchmarks. They care whether the agent handles their refund or their account correctly, every time, and knows when to hand off to a person. Sierra was working on that problem directly, and what convinced me was how seriously they treated the hard parts: evaluation, guardrails, and making agents something a company can own and keep improving. That's where I think agents actually become useful.

The timing mattered too. Building a capable agent is now feasible, but making one dependable is still an open engineering and research problem, and that's the kind of problem I find most interesting. I didn't want to study it only from the sidelines. I wanted to be where those tradeoffs get decided.
